summary.text: A Hertzsprung–Russell diagram is a scatter plot of stars that relates their luminosity or absolute magnitude to their classification or effective temperature.
In every form of the diagram, stars of greater luminosity sit toward the top and stars with higher surface temperature sit toward the left.
Created independently by Ejnar Hertzsprung and Henry Norris Russell, it was a major step towards understanding stellar evolution.

facts.label: Other name
facts.value: Sometimes called a color magnitude diagram

facts.label: Created
facts.value: By Hertzsprung in 1911 and independently by Russell in 1913

facts.label: Up the chart
facts.value: Stars of greater luminosity sit toward the top

facts.label: Across the chart
facts.value: Stars with higher surface temperature sit toward the left

facts.label: Cluster use
facts.value: Shows a cluster's stars without first knowing distance or luminosity

items.prompt: A star is plotted in the top-left corner of an H–R diagram. What does its position say about it?

options.label: Low luminosity and a high surface temperature
Low luminosity and a low surface temperature
High luminosity and a high surface temperature
High luminosity and a low surface temperature

items.explain: Greater luminosity is toward the top and higher surface temperature is toward the left.

items.prompt: An astronomer plots every star in one cluster by how bright each appears, yet can still compare the stars with each other. Why does that work?

options.label: They share one distance, so apparent and absolute magnitude differ by the same constant
Brightness as seen from Earth never depends on distance
Cluster stars all have the same luminosity
Cluster stars all have the same temperature

items.explain: Stars in a cluster are at identical distances, so a single constant, the distance modulus, separates apparent from absolute magnitude for all of them.

items.prompt: Hertzsprung saw that stars with narrow spectral lines drifted across the sky less than other stars of the same spectral class. What did he take that to mean?

options.label: The narrow-line stars were cooler
The narrow-line stars were hotter
The narrow-line stars were younger
The narrow-line stars were more luminous

items.explain: He took the smaller proper motions as a sign of greater luminosity for the narrow-line stars.

items.prompt: Why do astronomers make a sharp distinction between the theoretical diagram and the observational one, even though they look alike?

options.label: They plot completely different kinds of stars
Converting from one to the other is not trivial
One is drawn only for clusters
One has been shown to be wrong

items.explain: The exact transformation between them is not trivial; for example, going between temperature and colour needs a hard-to-build colour–temperature relation.

items.prompt: A chart puts the logarithm of surface gravity on the vertical axis and effective surface temperature on the horizontal axis. Which version of the H–R diagram is it?

options.label: The original spectral-type and visual magnitude diagram
The colour–magnitude diagram
The Kiel diagram
The cluster apparent-magnitude diagram

items.explain: The spectroscopic H–R diagram, also called the Kiel diagram, plots log g against effective surface temperature.

items.prompt: A modern observer builds a chart without using spectral types. What do they put on the horizontal axis in their place?

options.label: The star's name
The star's distance
The star's age
A colour index of the star

items.explain: Modern observational versions replace spectral type with a colour index, giving a colour–magnitude diagram.
